newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish tycoon details payments to ex-p.m. Haughey.
newsitem.headline: Irish tycoon details payments to ex-p.m. Haughey.

text.p: Irish tycoon Ben Dunne told a payments-to-politicians tribunal on Tuesday that he personally gave former prime minister Charles Haughey 200,000 pounds ($320,000) to help ease million-pound debts.
Dunne told the second day of the tribunal that the money was in the form of three bank drafts of about 70,000 pounds each and that he gave them to the former premier on one day in 1991.
But he said that he never expected "any favour or benefit" from Haughey, one of the most powerful figures in Irish politics for more than a decade.
By his account, the handover took place after Dunne played a round of golf near Haughey's home and dropped in "for a cup of tea" with three bank drafts in his pocket.
Dunne said the presence of the drafts in his pocket worried him throughout his golf game; he was concerned that they might fall out as he swung a club.
Dunne said that he handed over the drafts, saying: "There's something for yourself," to which Haughey replied; "Thank you, big fella (man)."
Dunne, former head of the Irish Dunne's department store chain, said that he understood that Haughey, prime minister four times until 1992, owed about one million pounds.

The counsel for the tribunal said on Monday that, between 1987 and 1991, Dunne handed over a total of 1.3 million pounds to Haughey, who has denied receiving any money in a letter to the judge overseeing the hearing.

The tribunal is investigating charges which have surfaced in the media and raised the political temperature in an election year. The tribunal says there is no allegation of any wrongdoing by anyone mentioned in the hearing.

The tribunal is investigating why Dunne, who was ousted from the family-owned chain in 1993, dispensed large sums of money to a variety of politicians. Dunne, now 58, said he gave hundreds of thousands of pounds to politicians including cash to help the election campaigns of Haughey's Fianna Fail party and its one-time ally, the Labour party.
His largesse also extended to money in exchange for the saying of masses and start-up money for job-creating projects including a theme park in the southern county of Kerry.
Michael Lowry of the ruling Fine Gael party resigned last December after admitting that Dunne paid for the quarter-million-pound renovation of his private home.

The tribunal is expected to sit for at least a few weeks. Bertie Ahern, current leader of the Fianna Fail opposition party, has called on Prime Minister John Bruton not to call elections before its work is over.
Bruton, leader of Fine Gael, is expected to call elections in late May or early June, several months ahead of the November deadline.
Fine Gael and its Labour party and Democratic Left coalition allies are currently six points behind the opposition in opinion polls.
